19.0.0.en: 1 Then Job answered and said, 2 How long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words? 3 These ten times have ye reproached me: ye are not ashamed that ye make yourselves strange to me. 4 And be it indeed that I have erred, mine error remaineth with myself. 5 If indeed ye will magnify yourselves against me, and plead against me my reproach: 6 Know now that God hath overthrown me, and hath compassed me with his net. 7 Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment.

19.1.0.en: How long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words [2]?

19.1.1.en: None of the bodily pains and calamities that befell Job held any psychological suffering like that which came upon his soul from his friends. The trials moved him to offer a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving to God, but the words of his friends crushed him. It is as though he cried out with the psalmist: "O Lord, heal me; for my bones are vexed" (Ps 6:2).

19.1.2.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees in the words of righteous Job here a rebuke addressed to his friends, who had almost destroyed his hope, which the devil had not been able to do to him. For the utmost that the enemy of good can do is to pour out upon him trials of bodily suffering that end in death. In all this Job does not care about the pains and does not fear death, since he sees in his battle with the devil that he receives a multitude of crowns as the trials increase. But his friends aimed their arrows not at his body, which will one day dissolve, but at his soul, to destroy his hope, and this is more dangerous. It is as though what the wicked friends did was more evil and more dangerous than what the enemy of good aimed against him.

19.1.3.en: The Holy Bible often speaks to us of the danger of violent words that shatter the soul, and it warns us as well of smooth words that hide a deadly, deceitful heart. The sharp tongue is a deadly arrow, and its blows are more dangerous than being killed by the sword or beaten with whips; and the lying tongue is set together with haughty eyes and hands that shed blood.

19.1.4.en: "Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue" (Sir 28:22).

19.1.5.en: "Their tongue is as an arrow shot out; it speaketh deceit: one speaketh peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth, but in heart he layeth his wait" (Jer 9:8).

19.1.6.en: "The stroke of the whip maketh marks in the flesh: but the stroke of the tongue breaketh the bones" (Sir 28:21).

19.1.7.en: "A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood" (Prov 6:17).

19.1.8.en: "A man of an ill tongue is dangerous in his city; and he that is rash in his talk shall be hated" (Sir 21:8).

19.1.9.en: "His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity" (Ps 10:7).

19.1.10.en: "The Lord shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things" (Ps 12:3).

19.1.11.en: "My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword" (Ps 57:4).

19.1.12.en: "Who will set a watch before my mouth, and a seal of wisdom upon my lips, that I fall not suddenly by them, and that my tongue destroy me not?" (Sir 22:33).

19.1.13.en: * The first commandment: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile" (Ps 34:13; 1 Pet 3:10). For the sin that the tongue causes is exceedingly active and many-sided, and it has its part in anger, vainglory, hypocrisy, condemnation and deceit. Would you have me list the many names of the sins of the tongue? For from the tongue come slander, mockery, extreme folly, false accusations, bitterness, oaths and false witness. The tongue is the inventor of all these evils and more.

19.1.14.en: St. Basil the Great * A horse cannot tame itself, and neither can a man do this. A man must necessarily tame a horse, and in the same way God must tame man.

19.1.15.en: St. Augustine * The sword kills the body, and the tongue kills the soul. The tongue knows no moderation: it is either very good or very evil. It is very good when it knows that Christ is God, and very evil when it denies this. Let no one deceive himself, thinking that he has never sinned, for I sin, and I do so with my tongue.

19.1.16.en: * The more the tongue sins, the more wretched it becomes!

19.1.17.en: St. Jerome * The practical proof of a sound mind and a perfect thought is that no error is found on our tongues, and that we keep our mouths shut when necessary. It is better that we be led by fitting speech, which is able to know and express the perfection of every praise. For the most useful of gifts is to be able to speak wisdom when talking about the good life. Evil speech must be foreign to the saints.

19.1.18.en: St. Cyril the Great * Guard the tip of your tongue, for it is like a royal steed. If a bridle is put in its mouth and you teach it to walk with discretion, it submits to this and is content. But if you leave it to run without restraint, it becomes a chariot for Satan and his angels.

19.1.19.en: * The tongue is a sharp sword. Let us not wound anyone with it, but rather cut with it the "gangrene" that is within us.

19.1.20.en: St. John Chrysostom * When the body is weary, I feel no pressing need; I count my pains as nothing, and I do not care for my body when this clay is spent and passes away. Do not torment my soul, and do not trouble my spirit, for since my soul carries a (spiritual) melody, my enemy is struck by it. I am victorious in the battle, and I do not fear the pains. But you crush me with your words, and you take from me the hope of obtaining the crowns, and you make me turn back my steps like one who has not run well.

19.1.21.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Understand the words of the holy man as spoken at one time about his own person, at another time by the tongue of the Head (Christ), and at another time as a type of the universal Church.

19.1.22.en: Now the soul of the righteous man is in deep sorrow when people hurl words against him without having learned to practice the good life, and with words they ascribe righteousness to themselves, though in practice they are his enemies...

19.1.23.en: Job speaks about his own person, so as to speak, confessing, with the tongue of the universal Church: "But in truth I am ignorant, and my ignorance is with me" [4 Vulgate]. It is as though he says of the heretics: "All your knowledge is not with you, but against you, since it lifts you up in foolish pride. But my ignorance is with me, for it works on my behalf, since I do not presume to inquire into the things of God with pride of heart. Keep my soul in the truth, in the spirit of humility..."

19.1.25.en: If the wounds of righteous Job were exceedingly bitter because of the harsh words of his friends, more than any other bitterness, then it is fitting for us, as believers who care for the safety of our brethren, their salvation and their joy in the Lord, not to utter wounding words, but to have good words that heal their wounds and comfort their hearts in the Lord. The Holy Bible urges us not only to guard against the sharp tongue, but also that God may grant us a gentle tongue that supports us and supports our brethren with its healing sweetness.

19.1.26.en: * The Apostle said this (Jas 3:8), not that we should be indulgent toward this evil of the tongue, but that we should ask for divine grace to tame our tongues.

19.1.27.en: St. Augustine * The fountain is the heart of man, the channel in which the water overflows is his speech, and the opening from which it comes out is his mouth. The sweet water is sound teaching, and the bitter water is that which is contrary to it.

19.1.28.en: Fr. Hilary, Bishop of Arles * It is a great thing to be able to control the tongue, for failure in this is the greatest of evils.

19.1.29.en: St. Cyril the Great "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Prov 16:24).

19.1.30.en: "He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour" (Ps 15:3).

19.1.31.en: "My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer" (Ps 45:1).

19.1.32.en: "A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit" (Prov 15:4).

19.1.33.en: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof" (Prov 18:21).

19.1.34.en: "By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone" (Prov 25:15).

19.1.35.en: "Be not hasty in thy tongue, and in thy deeds slack and remiss" (Sir 4:34).

19.1.36.en: "Sweet language will multiply friends: and a fair-speaking tongue will increase kind greetings" (Sir 6:5).

19.1.37.en: "If she have kindness and meekness in her tongue, her husband is not like other men" (Sir 36:25).

19.1.38.en: "The flute and the psaltery make sweet melody: but a pleasant tongue is above them both" (Sir 40:21).

19.1.39.en: These ten times have ye reproached me.

19.2.0.en: Ye are not ashamed that ye make yourselves strange to me (rebuke me) [3].

19.2.1.en: They put him to shame by the evil qualities they ascribed to him and by what they accused him of, time after time, without hesitation. Their words were like a deadly sword and like heavy stones that crushed his soul. They were not ashamed to despise him, for they made themselves strangers to him and pretended not to know him (Job 2:12). They did not deal with him with the same familiarity they had in his prosperity. Therefore the wise man says: "A friend loveth at all times" (Prov 17:17).

19.2.2.en: They had spoken five times, and each of them multiplied his reproach, so Job counted what they had done to him, saying: "These ten times have ye reproached me." The number ten points to completeness in time, which is why the commandments in the Law are ten, signifying the believer's obligation to the commandment throughout the span of his life. Here it is as though he did not leave the friends a single moment of their sitting with him without its carrying a spirit of biting criticism and rebuke with which to put him to shame.

19.2.3.en: * "Only that ye may know that the Lord dealeth thus with me" [3 LXX]. He says: at least let the honour of Him who disciplines me change your view of me. For it is not fitting for you to trample on people whom God disciplines, but to sigh and grieve over such, especially since it is not fitting for anyone to rejoice at another's death, for this conduct is not left without punishment.

19.2.4.en: St. John Chrysostom And be it indeed that I have erred.

19.3.1.en: "And be it indeed that I have erred" means: suppose that your accusations are true and that I have indeed erred, whether through ignorance or mistake, for every man is exposed to this, and this touches my own life; for my error - if I err deliberately, with malice and deceit - remains with me and not with you, so why all this deadly attack?

19.3.2.en: Perhaps it means: if I am truly in the wrong and wicked, and I suffer because of my wickedness, and all these calamities have come upon me, leave me in my bitterness; why do you add pains to my pains?

19.3.3.en: * [You rise up against me], as though he says to them: "It would have been fitting for you, on the occasion of my being struck (by trials), to rise up against yourselves. This is the good ordering of rising up on the side of what is good, that we stand first against ourselves, and afterward against the wicked. We rise up against ourselves when we look at our evil works, and strike ourselves with the harsh punishment of remorse, and never leave ourselves in our sins, and are not partial toward ourselves by any foolish thought.

19.3.4.en: We must first track down our evils within us with severity. Then it is just that we rise up to resist evil in others for their benefit, and the evil that we punish in ourselves we apply also to others...

19.3.5.en: The wicked know nothing of this kind of rising up, for they leave themselves alone and attack the righteous... Therefore it was rightly said to the friends of blessed Job, who were haughty toward him while he was under punishment: [You rise up against me]. In other words, it was said to them: "You leave yourselves, who deserve blame, and you rebuke me with harsh expressions." For whoever does not judge himself first does not know how to judge others rightly... So it was said to those who acted deceitfully when they brought an adulteress to fall under judgment: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her" (Jn 8:7). For they came to punish the sins of others and left their own sins behind them.

19.3.7.en: * "Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye"(a).

19.3.8.en: Remove hatred from yourself so that you may be able to correct the one you love. The Lord rightly says "Thou hypocrite," for only the man who loves may complain of the sins of others, whereas the wicked man, when he complains of others, is a hypocrite, since he shows himself in a form other than what he is... For there is a kind of pretenders who complain of the sins of others, such as hatred and grudge, with the aim of appearing to be men of counsel... Let us take care lest we fall into this. Likewise, if you are compelled to expose the faults of others or to rebuke them, let us look at ourselves to see whether we commit the same sins, or have committed them before. If we have not committed them, let us know that we are human beings exposed to sin. But if we have committed the sin before and have been freed from it, let us remember our weakness continually. Therefore we must hold love, not hatred, for those whose faults we expose... and let us take care lest we be occupied with their sins... Let us not blame the sinner or rebuke him, but grieve deeply over this state of ours, not asking him to obey us, but to strive together with us.

19.3.9.en: * We should use rebuke only rarely. And if we are compelled to use it, we must eagerly seek to serve God and not ourselves. Let us have one aim, so that we do nothing with a double heart. Let us take out of our eyes the beam of envy or malice or pretence, so that we may be able to see and take the mote out of our brother's eye. Let us look at the mote with the eyes of the dove, which belong to the bride of Christ (Song 1:4), whom God chose for Himself as a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle, that is, pure, with no guile in her (Eph 27:5).

19.3.10.en: St. Augustine * Christians must strive... not to judge anyone, not even one of the adulteresses, nor the wicked who are notorious for their sins, nor the disorderly, but to regard the whole human race with simplicity of intention and a pure eye, so that a man becomes by his nature and foundation one who despises no one and neither judges nor hates anyone, nor even makes distinctions among people. If you see a one-eyed man, do not despise him in your heart, but give him the attention that is his due, which you would have given him if he had no defect... For true purity of heart is that when you see sinners or the weak, you pity their state and show them mercy. For this is what befits the saints of the Lord, that they sit in the watchtower (Hab 2:1; Isa 21:8), and behold the error and deceit of the world, and speak to God by the inner man.

19.3.11.en: St. Macarius the Great * Do not wrong a man, who is the image of God, because of the evil in him, for evil is an accident, a trial, an illness and a satanic deception, but his being, as the image of God, remains.

19.4.0.en: Fr. John of Kronstadt If indeed ye will magnify yourselves against me, and plead against me my reproach [5].

19.4.1.en: Job felt that they had not only taken an inhuman stand toward him and turned away from his friendship, but that they had truly exalted themselves over him, counted themselves higher than he, and magnified themselves against him to humiliate him. Instead of removing his reproach from him, they confirmed his reproach as proof of his lack of integrity, sincerity and perfection. They took from his disgrace an argument to establish his wickedness.

19.4.2.en: The proud Pharisee saw in the adulterous woman an unbearable uncleanness and an intolerable evil, so that he thought it too much for her to dare to enter his house. It was as though he wished he could drive out our Lord Jesus so that such as these would not enter with Him. But our Lord Jesus saw in her broken heart and the tears of her eyes much love, and so He forgave her many sins.

19.4.3.en: And the crowds saw in Zacchaeus, the chief of the tax collectors, a traitorous man, a lover of money, who did not deserve to live among them; but the Lord Christ saw in him his longing for salvation and for freedom from material things, so that he deserved the entrance of the Lord of glory not only into his house but into his very heart.

19.4.4.en: The look of our holy Lord Jesus, who loves the soul that confesses its blackness, is: [Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair] (Song 1:15). But her sisters look at her blackness, and so she rebuked them, saying: "Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me" (Song 1:6).

19.4.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem holds that blessed Job, to whose righteousness God bore witness, cannot have erred; he who received wisdom from above does not utter what is foreign to the truth; there are no vain thoughts in him. And yet, even if he had erred, it was not fitting for his friends to exalt themselves over him while he was in humiliation.

19.4.6.en: It is as though he says to them: "Why do you deal arrogantly with a man in humiliation? Why do you attack a person who has collapsed to the ground? Why do you hurt a person whom you ought to have pitied and prayed for? And suppose that you do exalt yourselves over me, why do you exalt yourselves over God? For His surpassing providence rests upon me."

19.4.7.en: St. Cyprian says: [It is pride and arrogance for anyone to dare to think himself able to do what God did not grant even to the apostles, supposing that he can distinguish the tares from the wheat... And whoever thinks that he chooses the vessels of gold and silver, and despises and casts out the vessels of wood and earthenware, though the wooden vessels are not burned except on the day of the Lord by the consuming divine fire, and the earthen vessels are not broken in pieces except by Him to whom a rod of iron was given.]

19.4.8.en: * The Lord counsels us not to judge anyone rashly or unjustly, because He wishes us to do everything with a simple heart that is always turned toward God. This is so since the disposition of one who judges others is to search out the sins of others in order to rebuke and condemn them, not to correct and train them in love... all this because of their pride or envy; therefore the Lord of glory added: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?"

19.4.9.en: So if your brother falls into the sin of anger, you fall into the sin of hatred (by your condemnation of him). And there is a vast difference between anger and hatred, as between the mote and the beam. For hatred is anger grown chronic; with the passing of time the mote (anger) has grown so strong that it is rightly called a beam (hatred). For if you are angry with a man, you surely desire his return to the truth, but if you hate him, you cannot long for his return.

19.5.0.en: St. Augustine Know now that God hath overthrown me, and hath compassed me with his net [6].

19.5.1.en: Perhaps he wanted to say that what befell him was by God's permission, so his life was torn down and he fell into a net, like game in a hunter's net, and there is no escape. Leave God to judge me...

19.5.2.en: Some see here an allusion to what the Persians, Romans and Goths were accustomed to do in their battles. In some Roman battles one soldier held his sword and shield while beside him another held a spear and a net. The latter made every effort to throw the net over his opponent's head, and if he succeeded in this, he immediately dragged him by the net wound about his neck, which had a snare in it, pulling him along the ground and striking him with the spear in his hand. Once the net was thrown over his head and he was inside it, he became helpless and powerless, and his fate was in the hand of the victor.

19.5.3.en: Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard.

19.6.0.en: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment [7].

19.6.1.en: Job felt as though God had taken a stand against him and that there was nothing to explain what had befallen him. He feels that he is under wrong, and here he calls upon God, and God does not answer. It is as though he says to them: why do you trouble my soul and crush it? Leave me to cry to my God and to press Him, and He will explain to me the cause of what has befallen me.

19.6.2.en: * [Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard] [7]. This concerns Him who said to the officer who struck Him: "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me?" (Jn 18:23). It is clear that the judgment was neither upright nor just, for with the great number of judges, not one pronounced according to the truth.

19.6.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Perhaps Job's cries here were a type of the cry of the Lord Christ in the midst of His sufferings on the Cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Ps 22:1; Mt 27:46; Mk 15:34)

19.6.4.en: * In His most tender humanity, and through the form of a servant that He has, we learn what we despise here in this life and what we hope for in eternity. In His very sufferings, in which His proud enemies thought they were victorious, He took the words of our weakness, where our sinful nature was crucified with Him (Rom 6:6), in order to destroy the body of sin, saying: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"... And this is how the psalm began that was sung long ago as a prophecy of His sufferings, and an announcement of the grace by which He raises up His believers and sets them free.

19.6.5.en: St. Augustine * Since He (the incarnate Divine Word) took a human soul, He took also the feelings of the soul. As God He was not in pain, but as man He was able to suffer. He died not as God but as man. It was in a human voice that He cried: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" As man He spoke on the Cross, bearing with Him our terror. For in the midst of dangers we respond as human beings, counting ourselves forsaken. Therefore as man He suffered and wept and was crucified.

19.6.6.en: St. Ambrose * He was forsaken, because His humanity had to pass through death. It must be carefully and precisely observed that He gave up the spirit with a loud cry after He drank from the sponge filled with vinegar and offered to Him on a reed (Mt 27:46-48)... The fact that it was offered to Him to drink from a sponge on a reed means that He took from the bodies of the Gentiles the sins that had destroyed eternity, and turned our sins to Himself, so that He might unite us with His immortality.

19.7.0.en: 8 He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkness in my paths. 9 He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head. 10 He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone: and mine hope hath he removed like a tree. 11 He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies. 12 His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle.

19.7.1.en: He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkness in my paths [8].

19.7.2.en: He began to comment on the bitterness that God had permitted for him, hoping they would have mercy on him and leave him. He portrays God as one who blocks his way, not allowing him to pass to escape even by death, and as one who has made his path darkness, so that he does not know where to go. He reproaches God and asks Him about the secret behind these events.

19.7.3.en: Perhaps Job expected, in the midst of all the hardness of their hearts and their harshness with deadly words, to find at least a little tenderness, so he wanted to stir them so that they would cease what they were doing to him and have pity on his state.

19.7.4.en: * [He hath fenced up my way round about me, so that I cannot by any means escape]. This is because of the cohort of Pilate's soldiers and the crowd of the Jews. They "encompassed" the Lord, pursuing Him, as Pilate ordered (Mt 27:26-27). Some spat in His face (Mt 27:30), others struck Him with their hands (Jn 19:3), and others beat Him. In any case He did not escape from the midst of the people who surrounded Him...

19.7.5.en: [He hath set darkness before my face]. There was darkness from the sixth hour until the ninth. He took away the light of day, so that creation might not see the unveiled face of the Creator.

19.7.6.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * But the soldiers who gathered around Him were mocking Him. He became a laughingstock to them. "They look and shake their heads at me." His kingship appeared even in their mockery of Him, for they knelt before Him.

19.7.7.en: And before the Crucifixion the soldiers put on Him a robe of purple and a crown on His head. Why did they put a crown on Him, though it was of thorns? Because every king shows his kingship by means of his soldiers. So Jesus as King was crowned symbolically through the soldiers. For this reason the Scripture says in the Song of Songs: [Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him](b). The crown was a mystery, for He is the forgiver of sins and the remover of the curse.

19.7.8.en: Adam received this sentence: [Cursed is the ground for thy sake... thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee](c). For this reason it was fitting for Jesus to accept the thorns, so as to remove this sentence. And for this reason Jesus was buried in the earth, so that the earth that was cursed might receive the blessing instead of the curse.

19.7.9.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * The crucifiers stripped Him of His garments like shearers, but He was silent like the sheep before her shearer!

19.7.10.en: He left His garment in joy, so that those who went out of Paradise naked might put it on!

19.7.11.en: He clothes them with His garments and He Himself remains in mockery! For He knew that they were fit for exposed Adam!

19.7.12.en: They stripped off His garments and put on Him a scarlet robe, the colour of blood, that the slain Bridegroom might be adorned with it!

19.7.13.en: * They gave Him a reed to hold like a judge, and for their sake He was constrained to write the bill of divorce of the daughter of the Hebrews, because she hated Him!

19.7.14.en: She gave Him the reed to write her divorce, because she saw that He loves holiness greatly, like His Father.

19.7.15.en: * They blindfolded His eyes and mocked Him, and struck Him, and said to Him: Prophesy to us, who is it that smote thee!

19.7.16.en: They struck with the reed the exalted Head, and the angels were terrified!

19.7.17.en: With these corrupt and evil things they repaid Him in madness...!

19.7.18.en: They went mad in order to veil the face of the Sun of Righteousness, lest He shine, and the world see their corruption.

19.7.19.en: The foolish bride veiled the Bridegroom, lest He see her lewdness and corruption.

19.7.20.en: They veiled the Physician, lest He bind up their wounds and heal them!

19.7.21.en: Look at Christ, how much He endured from the wicked!

19.7.22.en: That fool, how did he dare to spit in His face!

19.8.0.en: St. Jacob of Serugh He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head [9].

19.8.1.en: It is as though God had taken from him his wealth and his former honour, and every opportunity for doing good, and his authority and his kingly crown, so that he became without strength.

19.8.2.en: Without doubt Job spoke these words in bitterness of heart, under the pressure of the severity of the trial, not in pride and arrogance against the judgments of God, but in bitterness and sorrow. For this reason, although the words seem to contain boldness, God looked to his meek spirit. As Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [He who ceases from his righteousness because of sorrow is not righteous, but blessed Job, because of his meek spirit, did not sin even in uttering harsh words. For if we say that he sinned by this saying, we make Satan to have achieved his purpose when he said: "Touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face" (Job 2:5).]

19.8.3.en: * "He hath stripped me of my glory" [9]. For there was need for the word of the prophet Isaiah to be fulfilled: [He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him... his visage was so marred more than any man] (cf. Isa 53:2-3).

19.8.4.en: [And taken the crown from my head], so that they might prepare for Him a new crown made of thorns (Mt 27:29).

19.8.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * He says: "He has stripped me of my glory," because the glory of every man is his righteousness. Now just as a garment protects from the cold, so righteousness protects from death. Thus it is not unfitting to liken righteousness to a garment, for it was said by the prophet: "Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness" (Ps 132:9).

19.8.7.en: * They plaited a crown of thorns and put it on Him. This is fitting for Him, for He came to uproot the thorns from the earth!

19.8.8.en: He bore the curse of the earth by the crown that they placed on His head, and bore the weight of the whole world like a mighty one!

19.8.9.en: Sins and transgressions, pains, sufferings and blows were plaited into the crown and set on His head that He might bear them!

19.8.10.en: And by the thorns the curse of Adam was loosed!

19.8.11.en: He became a curse, so that the heirs who return might be blessed through Him.

19.8.12.en: By His crown He uprooted the accursed seed of the serpent!

19.8.13.en: By His crown of thorns and the curse of the earth that killed the generations... He removed the curse of Adam and his sweat!

19.8.14.en: By the crown of thorns He pulled down the crown of Satan, who wished to be god over creation!

19.8.15.en: By His crown of thorns He plaited a crown for the daughter of the Gentiles, the bride whom He betrothed from among the idols and wrote in His name!

19.8.16.en: * The great Saviour was scourged, and by the sentence issued by the governor He went out to be crucified!

19.8.17.en: He came to His own, and His own received Him not, but cast Him out from among them with mockery!

19.8.18.en: He went out to die with the wicked without any fault; then Judas - the lamp that was put out from among his companions - repented and was ashamed of the evil deed that he had done.

19.8.19.en: He who betrayed Him returned the silver to those who had seized Him, since he despised himself, and confessed that he had betrayed Him with evil... and the crucifiers also fled like those who are not near, and said: What is that to us? See thou to that.

19.8.20.en: The pure blood cast terror upon those who shed it, and they began to be afraid and to tremble before it even before they shed it!

19.9.0.en: St. Jacob of Serugh He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone: and mine hope hath he removed like a tree [10].

19.9.1.en: He did not merely leave him in a closed way, nor as a humiliated slave, but pulled down his whole being on every side. It is as though he were a tree that had been uprooted. He became torn down on every side, and the devil heard this complaint, he of whom he had said that God had set a hedge about him and about his house and about all that he had on every side (Job 1:10).

19.9.2.en: * "He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone" [10]. This was when the disciples who had formerly been at His side were scattered (Mk 14:50). As for Himself, He delivered Himself to those who seized Him; He went!

19.9.3.en: [And mine hope hath he removed like a tree]. He did not say that He uprooted it from its roots, but that He cut it off, for when a tree suffers somewhere above the roots, other trees come forth from the root after it is cut.

19.9.4.en: As soon as Christ was crucified, the hope that many had in Him was cut off, although He had spoken with His disciples before about His resurrection (Mt 16:21). Since they were troubled by His sufferings, they despaired of the Saviour.

19.9.5.en: This is exactly what happened when Cleopas said: "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel" (Lk 24:21). The Saviour rebuked him firmly for reaching this degree of despair, when Christ said: "O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken" (Lk 24:25). And since He showed that there was no need to lose hope in Him, He added: "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?" (Lk 24:26).

19.9.6.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Despair almost mastered Job when trials surrounded him on every side, and he became like a tree that had been cut down, yet its root stayed alive, so that it returns and puts forth small shoots that grow and flourish. As for the Lord Christ, all rose up against Him, He was sentenced to death, and those around Him almost lost hope in what they had expected of Him as the Saviour of Israel.

19.9.7.en: Now when tribulations surround the Church and some of the weak fall, some think that she fails in her mission. But God, who permits her troubles so that she appears like a tree cut down, is her support; He works by His Holy Spirit in her, so that she gains many through weakness, and remains in the world like the leaven that seems to have died in the midst of the dough, yet leavens the whole dough! So it is fitting for us not to lose hope, but always to rejoice in those who join her to enjoy eternal salvation, through the living word of God.

19.9.8.en: * The Church is torn down on every side as she is dissolved in her weak members, when those who appear to be strong perish. And the crown is taken from the head, in the sense that the eternal rewards are neglected by those who occupy the place of the head. Therefore he rightly adds, concerning the fall of the weak: "And mine hope hath he removed like a tree."

19.9.10.en: * Leaven is a small quantity, but it takes hold of the dough and spreads through all of it, and quickly passes on to it all its properties. The word of God works in us in a similar way, for when we receive it within us, it makes us holy and blameless.

19.10.0.en: St. Cyril the Great He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies [11].

19.10.1.en: The wrath of God upon Job became like a fire that was kindled, and it blazed and burned him. It is as though he cries out with the psalmist: "Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand" (Ps 39:10).

19.10.2.en: This is what was prefigured when Moses struck the rock with the rod. "Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel" (Ex 17:6). It is said: "And Moses lifted up his hand, and with his rod he smote the rock twice: and the water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their beasts also" (Num 20:11). Therefore the psalmist says: "He opened the rock, and the waters gushed out; they ran in the dry places like a river" (Ps 105:41). "Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters" (Ps 114:8).

19.10.3.en: This is what the prophet Isaiah saw in the Lord Christ on the Cross, when he said: "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:4-5).

19.10.4.en: * "He hath also kindled his wrath against me," by the condemnation of Adam. The new (Adam) came (1 Cor 15:45) to pay the debt (Col 2:14) of the old Adam. For this reason Job added: [And he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies]. It is clear that He demanded from me the debt that is upon the disobedient.

19.10.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * To be sure that it is He Himself whom Moses saw, hear the testimony of Paul, who says: "For they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 4:10).

19.10.6.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * For those, water burst forth from the rock, but for you blood flows from Christ. The water was enough for them for an hour, but today He waters you for eternity.

19.10.7.en: St. Ambrose * Consider the word of the Creator and liken it to the rock that went with the people of Israel in the wilderness. It was not a reservoir of water that held within it what flowed out upon them in glorious streams. There was no water in the rock, but oceans welled up from it. Such is the act of the Word, who formed creatures out of nothing.

19.10.8.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian * Again the cloud rose up and led them to another place (Ex 17:1-7). But this place was a barren desert with burning sands, and there was not a drop of water in it. And here again thirst afflicted the people. But when Moses struck a protruding rock with his rod, it brought forth sweet water, good to drink, in greater abundance than all this great multitude needed.

19.10.9.en: * It is not difficult to reconcile the historical sequence with the spiritual contemplation. The man who left the Egyptians dead behind him in the water, and was purified by the wood, and delighted in the springs of the disciples, and rested in the shade of the palm trees, is indeed able to receive God. For the rock, as the Apostle says, is Jesus Christ. And this rock is hard and resistant to unbelievers, but if a man uses the rod of faith, the rock turns into water for the thirsty, and flows to those who receive the Lord Christ, for He says: "(I and my Father) will come unto him, and make our abode with him" (Jn 14:23).

19.10.10.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * The rock was struck twice with the rod so that it might pour out water, because the Cross has two beams. All these things, then, were done as a type, and they have been revealed to us.

19.11.0.en: St. Augustine His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle [12].

19.11.1.en: The attack of the raiders upon him was by God's permission, so he called them "God's raiders" or "His troops." They came to him without hindrance and encamped around his tent without resistance. They besieged him like an army that deprives a city of provisions until it perishes of hunger and thirst!

19.11.2.en: * It often happens that evil spirits instil many things into the hearts of those who suffer, and along with the blows that come upon them from outside, they instil evil thoughts in their hearts, calling down the wrath of God. Therefore it is rightly added: [The robbers come together, and make themselves a way through me] (Job 19:12). His robbers are the evil spirits who are busy hunting for the death of men. These make themselves a way in the hearts of the sorrowful when they suffer from outside because of dangers, and do not cease to pour in evil thoughts as well. Of these it was said: "They encamp round about my tabernacle" (Job 19:12)... and that is when they surround the mind on every side with temptations...

19.11.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is strange: why does he speak of robbers (raiders) and add that they are his, showing that these raiders are ascribed to him? In this place we must distinguish between the authority of the evil spirits and their will, for this shows why he calls them "God's robbers." For the evil spirits always pant and run to do us harm, but they have no authority to harm us unless they receive permission from the supreme will. Of themselves they long to harm us unjustly, but by Almighty God they cannot harm anyone except through justice.

19.11.5.en: * The devil planned not to draw us away from the blessings that we have, but he tries to draw us to a steeper cliff. But God in His love did not fail to care for mankind.

19.11.6.en: He showed the devil how foolish he is in his attempts. He showed man the greatness of the care that God shows him, for by death He gave man eternal life. The devil drew man out of Paradise, and God led him to heaven. So the gain is far greater than the loss.

19.11.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * Satan's temptations are directed all the more against those who have been sanctified, because he longs all the more to gain victory over the righteous.

19.12.0.en: 13 He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me. 14 My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me. 15 They that dwell in mine house, and my maids, count me for a stranger: I am an alien in their sight. 16 I called my servant, and he gave me no answer; I intreated him with my mouth. 17 My breath is strange to my wife, though I intreated for the children's sake of mine own body. 18 Yea, young children despised me; I arose, and they spake against me. 19 All my inward friends abhorred me: and they whom I loved are turned against me.

19.12.1.en: He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me [13].

19.12.2.en: Our Lord Jesus Christ did not come into this world to reject the Jews, His own, but through their unbelief He opened the doors of faith to the Gentiles.

19.12.3.en: * [My brethren are gone far from me, and they that knew me are strangers to me] (Job 19:13) LXX. The grace of the Gospel bears witness to this... for John says of the Lord: "For neither did his brethren believe in him" (Jn 7:5), when they said to Him: "Depart hence, and go into Judaea, that thy disciples also may see the works that thou doest" (Jn 7:3-4). They said this because they did not know His power, [and they knew strangers more than Him]. This is what the Jews saw plainly.

19.12.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Consider John's saying: "He came unto his own," not because of any need of Christ, for it is impossible for the divine Self to be in need, but He came for the sake of doing good to His own.

19.12.5.en: John made the blame of these Jews sharper when he said: "and his own received him not." Although Christ is the one who came to them for their benefit, they rejected Him, and they did not do this to Him only, but cast Him out of His vineyard and killed Him.

19.12.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * I will show this more easily when we bring forward the testimony of John, who says: [He came unto his own, and his own received him not] (Jn 1:11), for His brethren departed far from Him, and His acquaintances became strangers to Him. These are the Hebrews, who had the Law and were taught prophecy, and yet when He was present they did not know Him at all.

19.12.8.en: * He did not come with the aim of bringing about the unbelief of the Jews. But by His foreknowledge of what was to happen, He used beforehand the denial of the Jews and told us what would happen, namely the calling of the Gentiles to the faith.

19.12.9.en: The divine economy was wonderful... for He used the sin of the Jews to call the Gentiles into the Kingdom of God through Christ, though they were strangers from the covenants of promise (Eph 12:2).

19.13.0.en: Origen My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me [14].

19.13.1.en: God permitted that his relatives and acquaintances should not return his love, but the spirit of kinship, brotherhood, friendship, kindness and tenderness departed from them. They gave him their backs and not their faces, forgot him as though he had no existence in their lives, and cared nothing for any blood relationship or old friendship. They failed him, since he lost all hope in them. They were not moved by all the calamities that had come upon him.

19.13.2.en: * Not only was there no one to soothe his pains, but many frustrated him on every side with mocking rebukes. For the nature of trials is not such that those who rebuke us for them should stir up and agitate our souls. You see the bitterness of his grief and his saying: "Even ye have fallen upon me" (Job 5:19) LXX. And he called them "cruel," saying: my kinsfolk have failed, and my servants have conspired against me, I called the sons of my concubines and they went far from me (cf. Job 19:14, 17)... Some mock, others rebuke, and some despise, not only enemies but even friends. Not only friends, but even servants, who not only mock and rebuke but are also disgusted with him. And this not for two or three days or ten days but for several months... He found no rest even at night, and the terrors of the night were more fearful than the trials of the day. He suffered what was bitter in his sleep; hear what he says: [Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions] (Job 14:7). What man of iron or heart of steel could endure such miseries?
